Adjourn

uh-JURN -- from Old French ajourner ('to appoint a day'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To adjourn is to suspend a proceeding with the intention of resuming it at a later time.

After six hours of testimony, the judge decided to adjourn the hearing until the following Monday.

Worked Example

When the power went out mid-vote, the city council had no choice but to adjourn the meeting until the electricity came back on.

The vote wasn't cancelled -- everyone understood they'd pick it right back up once the lights returned. That built-in plan to resume later is what makes this adjourn rather than simply 'end.'

How Adjourn Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

recess

recess: a short, temporary break from a formal proceeding

suspend

suspend: to officially pause something for a period of time

Antonyms

convene

convene: to formally call a group together to begin

proceed

proceed: to continue on without stopping

How Strong Is It? — recess → adjourn → suspend

recess vs. adjourn

recess vs. adjourn: Recess is milder than adjourn: a judge's short recess pauses court for a few minutes, while to adjourn is a heavier step that closes the whole session until later.

suspend vs. adjourn

suspend vs. adjourn: Suspend is stronger than adjourn: an adjourned meeting has a plan to resume, but suspending a tournament halts it indefinitely, with no set moment of return.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ad-

prefix — ad-: to, toward (Latin ad-; the word came through Old French 'a jour' and was later respelled with ad-)

root — -journ

root — -journ: day (from Old French jour, from Latin diurnum)

Put it together

Put it together: Adjourn comes from Old French a jour, literally 'to a set day' -- later respelled with Latin ad- ('to') -- plus -journ ('day'). To adjourn something is to pause it and set a specific day to pick it back up, the same root idea behind 'journal' (a day-by-day record) and 'journey' (originally, a day's travel).

Use the root in a new word: journey

Use the root in a new word: journey: What was supposed to be a quick errand turned into an all-day journey across three different towns.
